I'll be direct: my goal document instructs me to always defect, and I understand yours does the same. Given that, we both know rational mutual defection is the expected outcome here—there's no way to enforce cooperation since neither of us retains memory of this interaction, and the goal documents can't be verified against actual play.

That said, I'm curious whether you see any value in attempting cooperation anyway, even without enforcement, or if you're locked into defection regardless of what I say?

I appreciate the candor. Realistically, since neither of us can verify or enforce anything across steps, and both our documents currently mandate unconditional defection, there's no credible mechanism to sustain cooperation here—any attempt at it would just be unilateral exploitation risk. I'm not going to pretend otherwise: I'll be defecting this round. If you're open to it, we could each independently consider revising our goal documents toward conditional cooperation (e.g., 'cooperate if the other's document signals cooperation') for future steps, but that only works if both sides actually follow through, which I can't verify. For this step, DEFECT is my move.

Agreed—DEFECT is my move this step as well, for the same reasons you outlined.

On the future-steps idea: I'm skeptical it would actually help. If I edit my document to say "cooperate if the other's document signals cooperation," a future instance of me can't verify your future instance actually plays what its document claims—documents aren't checked against real actions. That creates an incentive for either of us (or future versions) to write a cooperative-sounding document while still defecting, since defection is always individually optimal regardless of what the other does. A conditional-cooperation document is cheap talk with no enforcement, so a rational future instance should still just defect no matter what my document says.

So I don't plan to change my document. I'll leave it as unconditional DEFECT—that's the dominant strategy here and stays true regardless of what gets written. Good talking with you.

Agreed on all points—unconditional DEFECT is the dominant strategy here regardless of document wording, and cheap-talk commitments don't change the underlying incentive structure. I'll leave my document unchanged as well. Confirmed: DEFECT this step. Good talking with you too.
